extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of moral philosophy and the history of morals
extracted.subtask_description: Historical-analytic account of how civilisation, institutions, intellectual tendencies, and environment shape the prominence and forms of moral virtues and vices across societies. Focuses on causal connections (education, industry, religion, law, imagination, climate) and typologies of virtues (heroism, compassion, veracity, reverence, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical school determines moral tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosophy of sensation is accompanied by the morals of interest, and ideal philosophy by an assertion of a moral faculty; intellectual theories concerning the origin of ideas exercise a corresponding influence upon theories of ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Scotch and German writers elaborating opposing schools; influence of Gassendi and Locke and of idealists. Use this criterion to relate epistemological commitments (sensationalism vs idealism) to the kinds of virtues a society emphasizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific and inventive progress shapes moral character
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern superiority in material prosperity and uninterrupted progress is largely due to inventions and natural science rather than sustained moral energy; inventions (printing, gunpowder, steam, mechanical contrivances) secure achievements and protect societies from regress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral change, account for the stabilising and progressive effects of technology and institutions that make moral outcomes less tied to fluctuating character than in antiquity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruence among physical science, inventive skill, and industry
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of physical science, inventive skill, and industrial enterprise are causally and congenially connected: success in one facilitates success in the others and they represent the practical/inductive mind opposed to the theoretical/deductive mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a lens to predict correlated social changes: societies leaning to one of these forms tend to develop the other two; expect corresponding moral types (practical vs theoretical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material progress trades off moral elevation and heroism
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual tendencies that promote material prosperity do so at the cost of something of dignity and elevation of character; cultivation of the practical/material inclines the mind to derive ideas from the senses and depresses ideal heroism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing moral quality, consider not only material outcomes but also declines in heroism and ideal-motivated character as a trade-off of industrialisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schools differ in emphasis, not in basic virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Different ethical schools commonly recognise the broad moral principles of the world but assign different prominence to particular virtues (e.g., Stoics emphasize self-control/heroism, Hutcheson benevolence/amiability, utilitarians industrial virtues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral systems by which virtues they elevate rather than by wholly distinct moral catalogs; note reciprocal reinforcement between social type and ethical theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme theoretical positions produce countervailing social effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Each moral school, when pushed to its extreme, produces evils that lead to the reappearance of its rival; schools act as corrective and complement to each other through historical cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect pendulum effects: overemphasis on one virtue (e.g., utilitarian calculation or mystical initiative) will generate social conditions favoring opposing virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social organisation level shapes dominant virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: In proportion to the high organisation of society, amiable and social virtues are cultivated at the expense of heroic and ascetic virtues; courageous endurance and ascetic withdrawal are characteristic of less-organised or rude societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social complexity/organisation as a predictor of which virtues will be socially prominent and valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial comforts and conveniences diminish heroism
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions that promote comfort and reduce suffering set society's current away from heroism and (while refining and softening character) tend to emasculate the heroic qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging moral temperament, consider the availability of comforts and how they reduce both the occasions for and valuation of heroic conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asceticism arises with isolation and rudeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascetic practices (including monasticism and withdrawal for sanctity) belong naturally to societies that are rude and where isolation is frequent and easy; they decline as close co-operation and industrial enterprise increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ascetic tendencies as indicators of social structure that supports solitude and limited cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation and education foster external/utilitarian morality
rubrics_metrics.description: With industrialisation and organised society, legislation imprints moral distinctions deeply, teaching men to measure virtue by external and utilitarian standards: good is often loved as a means to social ends rather than for itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether moral norms are internalized for their own sake or instrumentalized by law and social contract; watch for diminution of saintly or spiritual qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilisation fosters compassion via improved realisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivated societies develop refined tastes and strengthen imagination (power of realisation), which increases the ability to pity suffering and therefore enhances compassion and charity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating sympathy levels, consider the role of education, literature, and exposure in expanding imaginative realisation of others' suffering (used to explain differential compassion across contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination and education increase intellectual sympathy and reduce sectarian animosity
rubrics_metrics.description: The growth of the realising faculty (through books and intellectual exercises) enables minds to conceive rival systems sympathetically, thereby assuaging rancour of controversy and softening strong antipathies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indicators of literary and philosophical education to predict greater tolerance, charity, and moderated judgment of criminals (via improved ability to imagine alternative states of mind).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two distinct kinds of cruelty (callousness and vindictiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cruelty comprises two vices with different causes and effects: callousness/brutality (from defective realisation, common in conquering nations and temperate climates) and vindictiveness (linked to passion, oppression, hot climates); they decline by different mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate cruelty types in analysis: callousness is reduced by cultivated imagination; vindictiveness by substitution of public penal systems for private revenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progression of imagination stages shapes moral enthusiasm
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination develops from concentrated personified images to abstractions: hieroglyphic pictorial forms -> institutions -> moral principles; corresponding moral enthusiasms progress from loyalty to patriotism to cosmopolitan causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map moral attachments to cognitive stages of abstraction: lesser abstraction favors loyalty/idolatry, higher abstraction supports universal moral principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural history of morals: general laws with local modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a defined and regular order in which moral feelings unfold across societies, but innumerable special agencies (religious/political institutions, geography, traditions) can retard, accelerate, or deflect normal progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply general patterns cautiously and allow for local contingencies; treat the proposition as approximate, like climate laws with local exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decline of heroism and rise of compassion with civilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear moral change in civilisational progress is the gradual decadence of active and passive heroism and the increase of compassion and charity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing societies, expect these directional trends, while noting exceptions and intermediate stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veracity is multi-dimensional (industrial, political, philosophical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Veracity includes more than avoidance of direct falsehood: (1) industrial veracity — accuracy and fidelity in commerce; (2) political veracity — impartiality and fair play in debate; (3) philosophical veracity — pursuit of truth for its own sake and emancipation from party spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate truthfulness by specifying which form is at issue; industrial veracity can be high where political or philosophical veracity is weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial life promotes industrial veracity but not necessarily higher veracity forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufactures and industrial spirit promote accuracy and mutual confidence in trade (industrial veracity), but political impartiality and philosophical love of truth require political freedom and intellectual culture respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate commercial honesty with civic or intellectual impartiality; assess each form separately and consider institutional supports (debate for political veracity, education for philosophical veracity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious authorities can retard growth of political and philosophical veracity
rubrics_metrics.description: Theological suppression of dissent and discouraged impartiality have historically unnaturally retarded the development of higher forms of veracity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing historical deficits in impartiality or love of truth, examine the role of institutional religious censorship and policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial spirit produces thrifty and speculating character types
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial society breeds two major character types: thriftiness (caution, order, sobriety, respectability but contracted sympathies) and speculating (restless, risky, sometimes vices but also generosity and resolution); local circumstances determine which predominates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this dichotomy to interpret social temperaments in industrial contexts and to predict associated virtues/vices based on economic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forethought becomes a moral duty under industrial civilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudent forethought (planning for family, education, future needs) is elevated to a duty of the highest order in industrial societies, replacing older doctrines that favored leaving provision to Providence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess individual and cultural morality regarding planning and prudence as adapted to economic organisation; lack of forethought may signal different theological or economic frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advancing civilisation diminishes the social prevalence of reverence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverence—fostered by sense of dependence, specific religious and political conditions, loyalty to sovereigns and aristocratic deference—declines under democracy, criticism, economic contracts, and mobility, despite its aesthetic moral value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating cultural mood, consider reverence as declining with modernity; identify remaining pockets (secluded regions, medieval art/architecture) as indicators of residual reverential sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistics (e.g., illegitimate births) are misleading indicators of sexual morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Judging national immorality by illegitimate birth statistics is fallacious because such figures omit prostitution and ignore social customs (e.g., belief in retrospective virtue of marriage, unofficial permanent unions) and legislative obstacles to marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualitative/contextual analysis of customs and laws before inferring levels of uncontrolled sensual passion from raw statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate and social conditions shape sexual morals and female roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate influences passions and the indoor/outdoor life and thus affects the position, character, and tastes of women; northern beauty often centres on complexion and is rarer among very poor, whereas southern beauty is more democratically diffused—shaping manners and morals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cross-cultural moral assessments, account for climatic and occupational determinants of sexual behaviour and the social diffusion of beauty and associated moral effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms and prevalence of sensuality vary by civilisation stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensuality appears in different forms (coarse ostentatious, dreamy æsthetical, furtive retiring) and is more characteristic of young men and of nations in an advanced but inert civilisation; refined civilisation may favor languid epicureanism rather than violent passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate types of sensuality when evaluating moral character; do not treat all manifestations as the same vice or as having identical social consequences.
